name: Plumbago Slate
lede: Plumbago Slate is a darker, bluer cousin of Plumbago Grey, named for the same shrub-or-graphite word but pushed toward true slate.

sections.title: Darker than its sibling
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary records this name on plate 46 D 6, with a first recorded date of 1912 [1]. It shares its root word with [[plumbago-grey|Plumbago Grey]], which Ridgway recorded that same year, but reads noticeably darker and more purple; where Plumbago Grey sits at lightness 62, this one drops to 42 [1][2]. The ISCC-NBS system would call its block "dark purplish gray" [2].

The nearest named colors in our data are [[graphite-violet|Graphite violet]] and [[graphite-violet|Heliotrope-Slate]], tied at 2.6 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[deep-slate-violet|Deep Slate-Violet]] close behind [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Plumbago Slate appears in 196 of our 23,781 paintings, about 0.82 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 84, more common than 56 percent of our named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 24 of 1,674 paintings, at 2.9 times the expected rate for that century, and is most over-represented in French paintings, at 2.1 times expected [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a shadow, in 31 percent of the 84 paintings where it carries real area [3].

The earliest match is dated 1445, in a work by Nicolás Francés — 485 years before Maerz and Paul's 1930 record of the name, as photographed, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. The latest dated match runs all the way to 2000[3].
